Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

impress verb

make an impression on someone

also be impressed, make an impression, impressed, leave an impression

classical

Traupman 100: maximē commoveō, make a deep impression on
Cic. Imp. Pomp. 23 (Lewis & Short)
Traupman 101, 154
Traupman 332

commoveō, commovēre, commōvī, commōtum

verb, second conjugation

move, stir; make an impression on

To move someone’s mind; in itself neutral, whether to fear, pity or admiration, so the context or an ablative says which (see affect).

Other words

  • admīrātiōnem suī injicere (+ dat.) — impress someone, fill someone with admiration

    also used · classical · Nep. Iph. 3: cuivīs injicere admīrātiōnem suī (Lewis & Short)

    Also admīrātiōnem movēre (Cic. Phil. 10.2: hoc mihi maximam admīrātiōnem movet). To be impressed by something is simply to admire it: mīror, admīror.

  • probō, probāre, probāvī, probātum — win approval for, make (something) acceptable to someone

    verb, first conjugation; aliquid alicui · also used · classical · Cic. Att. 4.14.1: quōs (librōs), ut spērō, tibi valdē probābō (Lewis & Short)

    Sē probāre alicui is to win someone’s good opinion, to make a good impression: multīs sē probāvit (Cic. Fin. 2.81, of Epicurus).

Examples

  • hoc mihi maximam admīrātiōnem movet

    this amazes me more than anythingCic. Phil. 10.2

See also affect, amaze, shock.

SourcesLewis & Short: commoveo · Lewis & Short: admiratio · Lewis & Short: probo

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, pp. 100, 101, 332.
